en.title: The Historical India–Nepal Borderland Economy
en.summary: The India–Nepal boundary across Mithila and the wider eastern Tarai/Madhesh did not create two self-contained economies. It cut across an older lowland–foothill–valley system in which cultivators, pastoralists, merchants, pilgrims, craftsmen, revenue farmers, carriers and state agents moved through linked markets and seasonal routes.

mai.title: भारत-नेपाल सीमांचलक ऐतिहासिक अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “भारत-नेपाल सीमांचलक ऐतिहासिक अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: A borderland economy existed before a fixed international line
Mithila, Tarai and Madhesh are overlapping historical frames, not synonyms
The corridor linked the Ganga plain, Tarai markets, foothill gates and Kathmandu
Patna’s importance came from aggregation, finance and connection to wider markets

en.title: Janakpur as Religious, Commercial and Urban Centre
en.summary: Janakpur’s historical importance cannot be reduced either to a sacred narrative or to a modern municipal chronology. The documented city emerged through the interaction of pilgrimage, temple institutions, ponds and ritual routes, cross-border exchange with north Bihar, transport infrastructure, administrative concentration and later urban growth. This chapter therefore treats Janakpur as a living urban system whose religious, commercial and civic functions repeatedly reinforced one another.

mai.title: धार्मिक, वाणिज्यिक आ नगरीय केन्द्र रूपमे जनकपुर
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “धार्मिक, वाणिज्यिक आ नगरीय केन्द्र रूपमे जनकपुर” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The historical method begins by separating sacred identification from urban chronology
Janakpur’s sacred geography created a framework for later urban concentration
Early modern traditions point to a renewed sacred centre, but exact dates require caution
Religious institutions were also landholding and service institutions

en.title: Land, Tenancy and Agrarian Society in the Nepal Tarai
en.summary: Agrarian society in the Nepal Tarai was created through the interaction of ecology, conquest, revenue policy, land reclamation, migration, tenancy and local intermediaries. The region cannot be described accurately by importing the Permanent Settlement model from British India or by treating terms such as raikar, birta, jagir and jimidari as interchangeable forms of landlord ownership.

mai.title: नेपाल तराईमे भूमि, किरायेदारी आ कृषक समाज
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “नेपाल तराईमे भूमि, किरायेदारी आ कृषक समाज” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Land history requires separating tenure, taxation and cultivation
The Tarai was an agrarian zone shaped by water, forest and disease as much as by law
Gorkha expansion incorporated Saptari and Mahottari into a wider revenue state
Raikar was the principal taxable framework, not a synonym for peasant ownership in the modern sense

en.title: Forest Clearance, Malaria Control and Demographic Transformation
en.summary: The demographic transformation of the Nepal Tarai after the 1950s was not the simple replacement of an empty jungle by settlers. The plains already contained towns, cultivated belts, forests, grazing grounds, pilgrimage routes and long-established Madhesi, Tharu and other communities. What changed rapidly was the relationship among disease ecology, forest access, state resettlement, spontaneous migration, roads, land law and agricultural expansion.

mai.title: वन-सफाइ, मलेरिया नियन्त्रण आ जनसांख्यिकीय परिवर्तन
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “वन-सफाइ, मलेरिया नियन्त्रण आ जनसांख्यिकीय परिवर्तन” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Demographic transformation must be reconstructed as a chain of linked processes, not a single malaria story
The pre-eradication Tarai was a mosaic of cultivated plains, forest belts, grasslands and settlements
Malaria shaped settlement ecology but did not exclude all lowland populations
Existing Madhesi and Tharu communities were actors in landscape making, not obstacles to later development

en.title: Migration and Settlement
en.summary: Migration and settlement transformed the Nepal Tarai/Madhesh after the middle of the twentieth century, but neither process began in an empty landscape. The plains already contained long-established villages, market towns, pilgrimage centres, cultivated tracts, forests and grazing zones linked across the India–Nepal border. What changed after the 1950s was the scale, direction and institutional framing of movement.

mai.title: प्रवासन आ बसावट
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “प्रवासन आ बसावट” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Migration and settlement are related processes, but they are not the same
The Tarai/Madhesh was inhabited long before post-1950 resettlement
Cross-border mobility with north Bihar preceded the modern development state
The 1950s altered the opportunity structure of lowland residence

en.title: Language, Education and Cultural Institutions in Nepal
en.summary: Language, education and cultural institutions in Nepal Mithila/Madhesh have never formed a single hierarchy. Maithili has long been a language of household life, ritual, literature, performance and cross-border communication, while Sanskrit, Nepali, Hindi, Urdu, Bhojpuri, Bajjika and English have occupied different institutional niches at different times.

mai.title: नेपालमे भाषा, शिक्षा आ सांस्कृतिक संस्थान
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “नेपालमे भाषा, शिक्षा आ सांस्कृतिक संस्थान” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Linguistic plurality in the Nepal Tarai predates the modern school system
Census language categories measure state classification as well as speech
Before mass education, learning moved through family, pathshala, monastery, mosque and apprenticeship
Rana-era education was narrow, and access to state-recognised schooling remained highly unequal

en.title: Gender, Citizenship and Household Economy in Madhesh
en.summary: Gender, citizenship and household economy meet most visibly where formal rights encounter everyday dependence. In Nepal Mithila/Madhesh, women’s economic position has been shaped not only by wages and land but also by marriage, migration, unpaid care, civil-registration documents, inheritance practice, access to schooling and the ability to move between household, market and public office.

mai.title: मधेशमे लैंगिकता, नागरिकता आ घरेलू अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मधेशमे लैंगिकता, नागरिकता आ घरेलू अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The household is an economic institution, not merely a private sphere
Women’s agricultural work has often been economically indispensable but statistically obscured
Unpaid care constrains time, mobility and the kinds of paid work women can accept
Marriage links property, residence and labour across households

en.title: Janakpur Art, Crafts and Cultural Economy
en.summary: Janakpur’s cultural economy is not simply a market for paintings. It joins ritual practice, women’s domestic knowledge, portable art, craft production, pilgrimage, tourism, institutional development, public murals, training, galleries, collectors and digital circulation. The same motif can move from a wedding wall to handmade paper, from a household threshold to a textile, ceramic object or urban mural, and from a devotional setting to a tourist purchase.

mai.title: जनकपुर कला, शिल्प आ सांस्कृतिक अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “जनकपुर कला, शिल्प आ सांस्कृतिक अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Cultural economy means more than the sale price of an object
The oldest economic foundation is unpaid domestic cultural labour
Ritual images create value by making places socially and cosmologically usable
Mithila art is internally diverse rather than a single timeless style

en.title: Border Markets, Remittances and Informal Exchange
en.summary: The India–Nepal border economy of Madhesh is neither wholly formal nor wholly informal. It is a layered system in which kinship travel, weekly markets, petty retail, commercial customs trade, labour mobility, remittance transfers, currency exchange and digital payments coexist. A person may cross the border legally without immigration formalities while the goods carried remain subject to customs rules.

mai.title: सीमा-बजार, विप्रेषण आ अनौपचारिक आदान-प्रदान
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “सीमा-बजार, विप्रेषण आ अनौपचारिक आदान-प्रदान” विषयक भारत-नेपाल सीमांचल, जनकपुर, भूमि, बसावट, भाषा, लैंगिकता, कला आ सीमा-बजारक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Border markets are institutions of a connected region
An open border for people is not a customs-free border for goods
Household geography routinely crosses the political boundary
Weekly haats and small bazaars remain basic price-discovery institutions
